context: Example 1. Fix d, C ∈ N. Define the instance space X = {x0 , ..., xd } and the label space Y = {0, ..., C − 1}. Let H1 = {0, 1}{x1 ,...,xd } and H2 = {x 7→ y 1{x = x0 } : y ∈ Y}. Consider the hypothesis class H = H1 ∪ H2 . Clearly, L(H) ≥ L(H1 ) = BL(H1 ) = d. Moreover, BL(H2 ) ≤ C − 1. We now give an upperbound on BL(H) by constructing a deterministic learner for H. Consider the learning algorithm that predicts 0 until its first mistake, removes inconsistent hypotheses, and plays the Bandit Standard Optimal Algorithm (BSOA) from Daniely et al. (2011) on future rounds. We now show that this algorithm makes at most 1 + max{d, C − 1} mistakes on any realizable stream. There are two cases to consider. Suppose the algorithm makes its first mistake on x0 . Then, by construction of H, the true hypothesis must be in H2 and thus the BSOA makes no more than BL(H2 ) ≤ C − 1 mistakes in all future rounds. On the other hand, if the algorithm makes its first mistake on x ∈ {x1 , ..., xd }, then the true hypothesis must be in H1 and thus the BSOA makes at most BL(H1 ) = d mistakes on all future rounds. Overall, the algorithm makes at most 1 + max{d, C − 1} mistakes. Since the BLdim lowerbounds the number of mistakes made by any deterministic learner under bandit feedback, we mustphave that BL(H) ≤ 1 + max{d, C − 1}. Taking C = d + 1, we have that BL(H) ≤ 1 + d ≤ 1 + L(H)C, which completes the example. We leave it as an interesting open question to derive optimal lower and upper bounds on the minimax expected regret in terms of only the BLdim (see Section 5).
